cover.topic: Catering orders, library tours, sustainable packaging and wool

sections.title: Ordering catering for a staff meeting
sections.context: You will hear a man phoning a café in Halifax to order lunch for a staff meeting.

transcript.speaker: Maureen
transcript.text: Pier Street Café, Maureen speaking.

transcript.speaker: Dylan
transcript.text: Oh, hello. I saw on your website that you do catering for events. I'd like to order lunch for a staff meeting at our office.

transcript.speaker: Maureen
transcript.text: Certainly. Let me bring up the catering order form. Is this for a company?

transcript.speaker: Dylan
transcript.text: Yes, it's an accounting firm. We hold a big meeting for all the staff twice a year, and this time I've been put in charge of the food.

transcript.speaker: Maureen
transcript.text: Lovely. Could I have your surname, please?

transcript.speaker: Dylan
transcript.text: It's Gallagher.

transcript.speaker: Maureen
transcript.text: And how do you spell that?

transcript.speaker: Dylan
transcript.text: G-A-L-L-A-G-H-E-R.

transcript.speaker: Maureen
transcript.text: Thank you, Mr Gallagher. And what date is the meeting?

transcript.speaker: Dylan
transcript.text: It's on Thursday, 13 November. Or, hold on. Let me check my diary. No, I'm sorry, they've moved it. It's Friday now, so it's 14 November.

transcript.speaker: Maureen
transcript.text: Friday 14 November. Good, we're not too busy that day. How many people should I plan for?

transcript.speaker: Dylan
transcript.text: At first I was told thirty. But a few more people from the Dartmouth office are coming, so it's now 36.

transcript.speaker: Maureen
transcript.text: Thirty-six. It's always better to order a little extra. Now, what would you like to eat? Our most popular lunch for groups is the soup and sandwich option, and the soup of the day is a seafood chowder, which is made with fresh haddock and scallops from Nova Scotia.

transcript.speaker: Dylan
transcript.text: That sounds perfect, and I'm sure a lot of people will want it. Is there anything for people who don't eat fish?

transcript.speaker: Maureen
transcript.text: Yes, there's a vegetable soup as well, and that's included. But I need to know about any special dietary needs in advance. Do any of your guests have allergies or other requirements?

transcript.speaker: Dylan
transcript.text: Two of them are vegetarian, which the vegetable soup covers. And one person can't eat wheat, so we need gluten-free meals for her.

transcript.speaker: Maureen
transcript.text: Fine. We make gluten-free bread, so we'll prepare one of those for her. I'll note that on the form. Do you want drinks as well?

transcript.speaker: Dylan
transcript.text: Just coffee and tea, if you can.

transcript.speaker: Maureen
transcript.text: Certainly. Now, the price. The soup, the sandwich platter and the coffee and tea come to 16 dollars per person. If you'd like dessert as well, we do lemon squares and fruit, and that brings it up to 18 dollars per person.

transcript.speaker: Dylan
transcript.text: I think we'd better have dessert. People always remember dessert. So, 18 dollars.

transcript.speaker: Maureen
transcript.text: Great, so 18 dollars a head, plus tax. The total comes to 648 dollars, before tax.

transcript.speaker: Dylan
transcript.text: Okay. And what time would you be able to deliver? The meeting starts at noon.

transcript.speaker: Maureen
transcript.text: We could come at 11:30, but the problem is that our van is out on another delivery until a quarter to twelve. So the earliest possible time is 11:45. Is that all right?

transcript.speaker: Dylan
transcript.text: That's a bit tight, but I think we can manage. I'll ask the others to set up the tables before then.

transcript.speaker: Maureen
transcript.text: Good. Where do we deliver to?

transcript.speaker: Dylan
transcript.text: We're at 250 Lorne Street.

transcript.speaker: Maureen
transcript.text: Was that 205?

transcript.speaker: Dylan
transcript.text: No, 250. Two, five, zero. It's on the third floor, and there's a lift.

transcript.speaker: Maureen
transcript.text: And the postal code?

transcript.speaker: Dylan
transcript.text: It's B3K 2R8. That's B as in Bravo, 3, K as in Kilo, 2, R as in Romeo, and 8.

transcript.speaker: Maureen
transcript.text: Thank you. I've got B3K 2R8. Now, for orders of this size we ask for a deposit when you confirm. For orders over five hundred dollars, it's 50 percent, but for smaller ones, it's a quarter. Yours is above that limit, so we need half.

transcript.speaker: Dylan
transcript.text: Oh, I thought it was less. So 50 percent?

transcript.speaker: Maureen
transcript.text: Actually, I've just looked at the notice on my screen. We changed the policy this month. The deposit is now 25 percent for every order, large or small, which is 162 dollars for yours.

transcript.speaker: Dylan
transcript.text: That's even better. Can I pay by card over the phone?

transcript.speaker: Maureen
transcript.text: Yes, I can take it now if you like, or you can pay online using the link in your confirmation email. Whichever you prefer.

transcript.speaker: Dylan
transcript.text: I'll pay online this afternoon, if that's all right.

transcript.speaker: Maureen
transcript.text: No problem. And one more thing. If you need to change the numbers, please let us know at least two days before the event, because we buy the fish fresh.

transcript.speaker: Dylan
transcript.text: Understood. Thank you so much for your help, Maureen.

transcript.speaker: Maureen
transcript.text: You're welcome. We'll see you on the fourteenth, Mr Gallagher.

sections.title: A tour of the Central Library
sections.context: You will hear a librarian giving a tour to new members of a public library in Winnipeg.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Central Library. My name's Fiona, and I'm the community librarian. I'm delighted to see so many new faces. Before we start the tour, I'd like to tell you a few practical things about becoming a member, and then we'll walk through the building floor by floor.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: First of all, joining. A library card is free for everyone who lives in the city, and all you need is a document showing your address, like a utility bill. If you live outside the city, you can still join, but there's an annual fee. Children can get their own card at any age, as long as a parent signs the form.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: Now, let me tell you about borrowing. Until recently, members could borrow twenty books at a time, but that was a bit limiting for the keen readers among you, so we've raised it to 30 books. The limit for DVDs hasn't changed. It's still five. There's a higher limit of fifty items for teachers, but that doesn't apply to most people.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: If you want to keep a book for longer, you can renew it. You used to be able to do this by phone, but we've closed the phone service, because hardly anyone was using it. Instead, you can renew online, using our website, or on the library app, which you can download for free. Of course, you can also renew your books at the desk, if you're here in person.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: Right, let's go on to the building. We start here, on the ground floor. This is the main entrance, and you can see the reading lounge on your left. It's where we keep the newspapers and magazines, and there are comfortable armchairs. Many regulars spend the whole morning here, and the café is next door, so you can bring a coffee in, as long as it has a lid.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: If you take the stairs or the lift, you'll find the first floor, which is the busiest part of the library. It's where you'll find our public computers, and a printing station. Using the computers is free for an hour a day, and you just need to sign in with your library card. Printing costs ten cents a page, and if you need help, a member of staff is always on duty.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: On the second floor we have the quiet study area, which is very popular with students. There are twelve small study pods, each with a desk and a power socket, and you can book one for up to three hours through the website. They're often fully booked during exams, so I suggest you plan ahead.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: The third floor is the most unusual, and it's my favourite. Here we have the local history archive, where you can look at old maps, photographs and newspapers from Winnipeg going back to the eighteen seventies. Some families come to trace their ancestors, and our archivist can help. It's open Tuesday to Saturday, and you need to make an appointment.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: You may have heard that there are plans for a makerspace with 3D printers and sewing machines. It's a lovely idea, but the funding has been delayed, so I'm afraid that it's been postponed. We'll announce it on the website when it's ready. And if you're looking for conversation groups for people who are learning English, those take place at the community centre next door on Wednesday evenings, not here.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: Finally, down in the lower level, we have the children's library. This is a bright space, with low shelves and beanbags, and there are storytelling sessions for the youngest children on Tuesday and Saturday mornings. Parents are welcome to stay, and there's a quiet corner for breastfeeding.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: Now, a few announcements. Some of you may remember paying fines for returning books late. I'm very pleased to say that we no longer charge late fees on any item. If you are late, we'll send you a reminder, and you simply can't borrow more until you've returned the overdue books. It's made a huge difference, and many people who had stopped visiting have come back.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: Another thing. Next month, the library will be closed on Monday mornings, as we're replacing the carpet on the first and second floors. We'll be open as usual in the afternoons. The notice is on the website, and we'll put signs on the doors. Sorry for any inconvenience.

transcript.speaker: Fiona
transcript.text: That's all from me for now. Please feel free to explore, and ask any of the staff if you can't find something. Enjoy the library.

sections.title: A marketing project on food packaging
sections.context: You will hear two business students, Ines and Marcus, discussing a marketing project with their tutor, Doctor Kowalski.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Kowalski
transcript.text: Good afternoon, Ines. Good afternoon, Marcus. I've read your outline for the marketing project. It's about reducing single-use packaging at the food trucks on campus, is that right?

transcript.speaker: Ines
transcript.text: That's right. We want to find out what would persuade students to use less packaging, and then recommend a plan to the truck owners.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Kowalski
transcript.text: Ines, what drew you to the topic?

transcript.speaker: Ines
transcript.text: I worked for a summer on a food truck in Halifax. At the end of every shift we threw away bags and bags of containers and cups, and I thought there must be a better way. The owner was interested, but he said he didn't know what customers wanted.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: And for me it was more about the business side. I think sustainability will be a big selling point in the next few years.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Kowalski
transcript.text: Good. Now, tell me about the survey you're planning.

transcript.speaker: Ines
transcript.text: We'll ask about two hundred students whether they'd prefer reusable containers, and what they'd be willing to pay.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: I'm a bit worried about that, though. People often say they care about the environment, but when it comes to paying fifty cents extra, they behave differently. So the survey might give us an over-optimistic picture.

transcript.speaker: Ines
transcript.text: But we can't really observe what they'd do without actually running a trial.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Kowalski
transcript.text: That's a fair point, Marcus, and it's a well-known problem in market research. I'd suggest you do both. Use the survey to find out what people say, then spend two lunchtimes watching what they actually do at the trucks. Count how many people bring their own cups, for example. That would give you a much stronger result than interviewing the owners, which I know you were considering.

transcript.speaker: Ines
transcript.text: I'd thought of the interviews because the owners know their customers well.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Kowalski
transcript.text: They do, and you might still talk to one or two. But it's the customers' behaviour that matters most.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Okay. Should we look at the different types of packaging in the report?

transcript.speaker: Doctor Kowalski
transcript.text: Yes, that would be useful. Let's go through the ones you've listed. Start with the paper cups.

transcript.speaker: Ines
transcript.text: We found that most of them have a thin plastic lining, so they look recyclable, but they aren't.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Kowalski
transcript.text: Exactly. In most Canadian cities, they can't be recycled, because the plastic can't be separated from the paper. That surprises many people, so it's worth explaining carefully.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Then there are the compostable containers. They're the obvious solution, but they cost nearly three times as much as plastic.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Kowalski
transcript.text: Which is a serious problem for a small business, with very thin margins. You'll need to show how the owners could afford it. What about the reusable bowls?

transcript.speaker: Ines
transcript.text: We thought we'd charge a deposit. The customer pays two dollars, and gets it back when they return the bowl.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Kowalski
transcript.text: It's a good model, but be careful about who returns them. In similar trials, it was mostly the regular customers who brought them back. Visitors and occasional customers tended to keep them, or throw them away.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: So the scheme only works if you have a loyal group.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Kowalski
transcript.text: Right. Next, the cardboard trays.

transcript.speaker: Ines
transcript.text: They're cheap and they're recyclable, but there's one problem.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: They go soggy. If you put hot food in them, like curry or noodles, they start to collapse within ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Kowalski
transcript.text: Precisely. Mention that, because it affects how customers see the product. And the wooden cutlery?

transcript.speaker: Ines
transcript.text: That's the surprise. In our pilot survey, it was the most popular change, because people thought it felt nicer than plastic, and it was only a tiny extra cost.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Kowalski
transcript.text: That's a useful finding, and an easy win for the owners. Now, what recommendations will you make at the end?

transcript.speaker: Ines
transcript.text: I think we should recommend a discount for people who bring their own cup. Even a small amount, like twenty cents, might change behaviour.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: And we could suggest a partnership with a composting company, so that the trucks don't have to dispose of the containers themselves.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Kowalski
transcript.text: Those are both realistic. What about banning single-use packaging altogether?

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: I'd like to, but the owners would never agree.

transcript.speaker: Ines
transcript.text: And a social media campaign could help, but it's not really the key.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Should we also include a section on the costs of our own recommendations?

transcript.speaker: Doctor Kowalski
transcript.text: Definitely. An owner will only act if he can see the numbers. Work out how many cups a truck sells in a week, what the discount would cost, and how much it would save on packaging. Even a rough calculation is better than none.

transcript.speaker: Ines
transcript.text: I could ask the owner I worked for. He'd probably let us see his sales figures if we promised not to publish his name.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Kowalski
transcript.text: That's a good idea, but get his agreement in writing. And think about the length of your report. The limit is four thousand words, and the best reports I see are usually closer to three thousand five hundred, with clear headings and short paragraphs.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: We'll aim for that.

transcript.speaker: Ines
transcript.text: What about the presentation? Should we use slides?

transcript.speaker: Doctor Kowalski
transcript.text: Yes, but keep them simple, with one main idea per slide, and perhaps a photograph from your observation days. A picture of a full rubbish bin makes the point better than a paragraph of text.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Kowalski
transcript.text: Agreed. Concentrate on the discount and the partnership. Send me a draft of the survey by next Wednesday, and I'll give you some feedback before you launch it.

sections.title: Wool: structure and sustainability
sections.context: You will hear a lecturer in textile science talking about the properties of wool.

transcript.speaker: Professor Quinn
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about wool, which is one of the oldest textile fibres in the world, and also one of the most interesting from a scientific point of view. Both Australia and New Zealand built their economies on wool, and it still matters a great deal to farmers in both countries, so I'd like us to understand why it behaves as it does.

transcript.speaker: Professor Quinn
transcript.text: Let me start with a little history. The sheep that produce the finest wool are called merinos, and they came originally from Spain. The first merinos arrived in Australia in 1797, brought by a small group of settlers, and within a few decades, the colony had become the world's largest producer of fine wool. The animals adapted very well to the dry climate, and the industry grew rapidly.

transcript.speaker: Professor Quinn
transcript.text: What does fine mean? The quality of wool is measured by the diameter of the individual fibres, in a unit called the micron, which is one thousandth of a millimetre. A human hair is about seventy microns across. The finest merino wool is less than 19 microns, which makes it soft enough to wear next to the skin. Coarser wool, which is used for carpets, can be more than thirty microns.

transcript.speaker: Professor Quinn
transcript.text: Now, what makes wool so special? Let's look at the structure. If you looked at a wool fibre under a microscope, you would see that its outer layer is made of overlapping scales, which together are called the cuticle. They are rather like the tiles on a roof. This is important for two reasons. It makes the fibre slightly water-repellent, so rain runs off, and it is also the reason wool can felt, which is what happens when a woollen jumper shrinks in a hot wash. The scales catch on each other and lock together.

transcript.speaker: Professor Quinn
transcript.text: Inside the fibre, there is another feature, which is the natural crimp, or waviness. Because the fibres are curly, they don't pack together tightly, and they form tiny pockets that trap air. That is why wool is such a good insulator. Air is a poor conductor of heat, so the trapped air keeps the warmth in on a cold day.

transcript.speaker: Professor Quinn
transcript.text: At the same time, the fibre is able to take in moisture. Wool can absorb up to 30 percent of its own weight in water vapour before it even feels damp. That's a lot more than cotton, and far more than synthetic fibres, which hardly absorb anything. This is why a wool garment keeps you comfortable when you sweat, instead of making you feel clammy.

transcript.speaker: Professor Quinn
transcript.text: Wool has some other useful properties. For one, it is naturally resistant to fire. It's hard to ignite, and when it does burn, it tends to go out by itself, so it's often used for uniforms and for furnishings in public buildings. It also resists odours, because the fibre doesn't hold bacteria in the way that synthetic fibres do.

transcript.speaker: Professor Quinn
transcript.text: Let's turn to sustainability, which is where wool has attracted a lot of interest recently. One concern with synthetic clothes is that every time they're washed, they release tiny pieces of plastic into the water. These are called microplastics, and they end up in rivers and oceans. Wool doesn't release microplastics, because it's a natural protein fibre, and in the right conditions, it breaks down in the soil, and returns nutrients.

transcript.speaker: Professor Quinn
transcript.text: However, we shouldn't be uncritical. Sheep farming has its own environmental costs, including methane emissions and land use. A typical merino sheep is shorn once a year, and it produces a fleece weighing about 4 kilograms, which is enough for several jumpers, but not a great deal in global terms. So the industry is working on reducing its emissions.

transcript.speaker: Professor Quinn
transcript.text: There has also been a lot of discussion about animal welfare. One issue concerns a practice called mulesing, in which a strip of skin is removed from around the sheep's tail area. The purpose is to prevent a serious condition called flystrike, which happens when flies lay their eggs on damp, dirty wool, and the maggots attack the animal. Mulesing is painful, and many consumers and retailers now refuse to buy wool from farms that practise it. Farmers are looking at alternatives, such as breeding sheep with smoother skin, or using better treatments.

transcript.speaker: Professor Quinn
transcript.text: Finally, a word about new uses. For decades, the main use of wool was clothing and carpets, but demand for those has fallen. In New Zealand and Australia, there is growing interest in using wool as building insulation. It's natural, it regulates humidity, and it doesn't release harmful dust. Several companies already sell wool insulation batts, and early results are promising, though they cost more than the standard fibreglass.

transcript.speaker: Professor Quinn
transcript.text: For next week, please read the two articles on the course page, and think about whether wool can compete with synthetic fibres on price, or whether it should be marketed purely as a premium product.
